title: Windblown lead carbonate as the main source of lead in blood of children from a seaside community: an example of local birds as "canaries in the mine".
ehr_evidence: The DoH undertook opportunistic sampling, taking blood from any resident who wished to have his or her PbB measured.
summary: In a cross-sectional isotope source-apportionment study of 49 children and 18 adults in the seaside community of Esperance, Western Australia, lead isotope ratios were used to attribute the proportion of blood lead derived from the Magellan mine lead carbonate concentrate.
key_findings: Mean blood lead (PbB) level in children was 7.5 µg/dL (range 1.5-25.7 µg/dL; n=49; geometric mean 6.6 µg/dL), with four children whose PbB was >12 µg/dL.
The contribution of Magellan mine Pb to PbB in young children ranged from 27% up to 93% (mean 64%, median 71%).
There was a significant positive relationship between PbB concentration and proportion of Magellan Pb (R2=0.12, p=0.018).
Subtraction of the Magellan ore component gave a mean background PbB of 2.3 µg/dL.
captured_features: Blood sample type (children, adults, cord blood)
pathologies_diseases: Lead exposure / lead poisoning (elevated blood lead levels)
study_design: Cross-sectional isotope source-apportionment study with opportunistic sampling
population: 49 children (48 aged <5 years) and 18 adults (>20 years), all living within 3 km of the Esperance port, Western Australia
limitations: Lack of isotopic data for environmental samples within individual houses, limiting identification of non-Magellan Pb sources.
Opportunistic, self-selected sampling biased toward higher PbB values.
Lack of knowledge of potential Pb sources other than the concentrate.
